item.title: When Feedback Becomes a Backdoor: Tracing Backdoor Skill Formation in Text-Space Skill Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reference answers are a supervision channel in text-space Skill optimization, which produces reusable text artifacts called Skills that guide future agent behavior. Poisoning those answers can induce a persistent trigger-conditioned rule without giving the attacker access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file. We study this reference-feedback poisoning in SkillOpt by tracing an attacker-supplied trigger--payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation. In SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, the natural attack retains an exact rule in all three seeds; each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered questions and 0/200 clean questions. In seed 42, removing the rule eliminates activation, and an in-run comparison shows similar clean accuracy to benign SkillOpt (169/200 versus 171/200). In SpreadsheetBench, where the payload requires an additional workbook edit, no natural run retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostic interventions locate two successive bottlenecks: the Analyst abstracts away required literals, and, once literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can remove exact edits before candidate construction. Poisoned references can therefore create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.
item.dc:creator: Louise Nayeong Koh, Yaechan Lee, Myeongjong Lee, Doyeon Kim, Juyoung Park, Seunggyu Kim, Inseo Kim, Chaerin Jung, Hyogon Ryu

item.title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.09375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data. Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.
item.dc:creator: Seyma Selcan Magara, Hanru Zhang, Fatme El Zahraa Hamad, Nico Pfeifer, Mete Akg\"un

item.title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
item.description: arXiv:2611.09422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Roy, Samar Parwez, Biswabandan Panda

item.title: Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.09446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu

item.title: Performance Bottlenecks in Computing ZK Proofs on a GPU
item.description: arXiv:2611.09569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to prove the correctness of a statement or execution of a computation while revealing no more than the statement of correctness itself. Recent use cases, such as AI datasets, suggest the need for faster proof generation over increasingly large constraint sets. This paper explores efforts in optimizing zero-knowledge proof generation, specifically PlonK, using GPUs, for applications that are not amenable to solution via incrementally verifiable computing (IVC). Our intention with this work is to improve ZK performance by introducing fundamental changes in the low-level architectural structure of proof generation. These changes affect performance curves for most current proof generation algorithms. In particular, this paper explores the trade-offs between increased parallelization on GPUs and the resultant memory management problems that occur due to this parallelization. We implement a parallelized PlonK in order to analyze these trade-offs and make arguments concerning the nature of data flows within the proving protocol. Our results lead us to consider multi-GPU environments to maximize performance for large circuit sizes. Such environments introduce issues of communication, efficient hardware management, data partition, and data transfers. This paper further discusses the use cases that motivate multi-GPU implementations, their cost models, and the use of remote direct memory access (RDMA) for data transfer among GPUs.
item.dc:creator: Victor Carolino, Caleb Geren, Michael Kaufman, Maximilian Nussbaum, William Scott, Henry F. Korth

item.title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
item.description: arXiv:2611.09607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Xia, Wenxin Xu, Taotao Wang

item.title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics
item.description: arXiv:2611.09658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.
item.dc:creator: Jie Fu, Yuan Hong, Yue Ning, Wendy Hui Wang

item.title: Empirical Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in SSH Infrastructure
item.description: arXiv:2611.09703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the anticipated arrival of Q-day, quantum computers threaten current cryptographic schemes for encryption and digital signatures. In response, major content delivery networks and cloud service providers are already adopting Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The current state-of-the-art focuses on benchmarking the operational performance of implementing PQC, but the real-world adoption status remains under-researched. This work utilizes large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool to analyze PQC adoption across 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities. Our study shows that the PQC transition in the SSH protocol is underway but highly polarized: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC, while 54.8% remain classical-only. At the entity level, 39.9% have enabled PQC on at least one host, whereas 60.1% have no PQC support. By correlating PQC adoption with industry, geography, and organizational size (digital and financial), this study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of PQC adoption status in SSH infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Md Ariful Haque, Sander Vinberg, Ben Edwards, Jo\~ao Cruz

item.title: Empirical Assessment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in TLS
item.description: arXiv:2611.09707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anticipating Q-day security concerns, major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While existing literature benchmarks PQC performance, empirical research evaluating real-world adoption data remains scarce. We present an empirical assessment of PQC deployment across seven critical protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP) using 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol. At the origin-server level, PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS, while falling below 1% for all other evaluated protocols. At the entity level, PQC support is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, while the remaining protocols have less than 5% of entities supporting PQC on the hosted servers. We further correlate these adoption trends against organizational digital and financial footprint, and industry sectors, yielding a multi-dimensional empirical assessment of PQC deployment. Finally, at the domain level, we perform a comparative analysis of PQC adoption in Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into the current state of PQC readiness over Transport Layer Security (TLS).
item.dc:creator: Md Ariful Haque, Sander Vinberg, Ben Edwards, Jo\~ao Cruz

item.title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
item.description: arXiv:2611.09721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
item.dc:creator: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi

item.title: GuardrailAgent: An Agentic Framework for Jailbreak Defense
item.description: arXiv:2611.09734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite undergoing safety training to align with human values, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that circumvent built-in safeguards and elicit malicious behaviors given by the adversary. Existing defenses are mostly static and fail to adapt to new or unknown attack strategies, providing limited resilience. To address these, we propose a multi-agent defense framework, GuardrailAgent, that offers adaptive, end-to-end protection. The system autonomously gathers and summarizes attack characteristics into a continuously updated knowledge base that supports both input- and output-side detection. A feedback module integrates misclassified cases for iterative improvement at minimal cost. Tested on over ten representative jailbreaks, the framework achieved a 93.1% input-side detection rate, 93.9% overall detection, and a 95.8% F1 score, while rapidly adapting to unseen attacks. These results demonstrate GuardrailAgent's outstanding capability to maintain LLM safety in the face of evolving jailbreak tactics.
item.dc:creator: Tianze Chang, Junjie Chu, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang

item.title: A Cross-Domain TARA-to-NAC Rule Mapping Methodology: From Automotive OEM Networks to Energy Storage Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Threat analysis and risk assessment under ISO/SAE 21434 ends with cybersecurity goals, but existing methods give little structured guidance for turning those goals into enforceable network access control rules. Compliance standards such as IEC 62443, ISO/SAE 21434, and ISO/IEC 27001 are usually applied as parallel efforts rather than as one enforcement architecture. This paper presents a six-step methodology that maps cybersecurity goals from a threat analysis and risk assessment to network access control rules, each placed at a named enforcement point and traceable to the threat records behind it. It also presents a unified compliance framework that treats IEC 62443 and ISO/IEC 27001 as a fixed substrate and domain-specific regulation as an interchangeable overlay. The methodology is applied to an automotive original equipment manufacturer plant network, addressing multi-tier supplier authorization and legacy operational technology devices, and then to utility-scale battery energy storage, where North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection standards and ISO/IEC 27019 replace the automotive-specific standard while the substrate stays constant. In the automotive example, 37 threat entries and 24 cybersecurity goals yield 23 rules covering 11 of the 13 in-scope goals; the energy example yields six rules. Three derived rules have no equivalent in the cited standards. Both examples are desk-based: the methodology is applied to them, not tested on them. The result is a reusable pattern for translating risk assessment into enforcement across critical infrastructure sectors, with empirical validation left as future work.
item.dc:creator: Krishna Teja Medam, Thiago Quinelato

item.title: PhotoFinish: Portable Timerless Probing of Microarchitectural Latencies
item.description: arXiv:2611.09879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Timing measurements are a fundamental building block of microarchitectural attacks, enabling software to convert otherwise invisible latency differences into architectural observations. Thus, restricting high-resolution timers is a common defense, especially in constrained environments such as web browsers. Timerless probing primitives provide an alternative approach. Instead of reading or constructing a timer, they observe architectural events that correlate with the microarchitectural state. However, such primitives typically rely on platform-specific behavior, and none generalizes across the wider computing landscape. In this paper, we present PhotoFinish, a portable timerless probing primitive that converts latency differences directly into an architectural value. PhotoFinish races an operation under test against a fixed reference in two parallel threads that then write unique values to the same shared location, resulting in a latency-dependent architectural value. PhotoFinish only requires parallel execution and shared memory, without constructing or reading a clock. We evaluate PhotoFinish on 38 CPUs spanning four ISAs and demonstrate reliable cache state classification across widely different microarchitectures, with comparable fidelity when compiled to WebAssembly and executed inside a browser. We further use PhotoFinish in AES T-table and Evict+Reload attacks, show that it applies beyond caches to TLB and execution-engine latencies, and demonstrate sufficient precision to identify the LLC slice of an address. Our results demonstrate shared-memory races as a generic and precise replacement for explicit timing, showing that restricting timers alone does not prevent software from observing fine-grained microarchitectural latency differences.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Hornetz, Eduard Ebert, Lorenz Hetterich, Lukas Gerlach, Michael Schwarz

item.title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training
item.description: arXiv:2611.09889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Nguyen, Dylan Gresham, Gaby G. Dagher, Min Long

item.title: Aegis OS: A Transactional Multi-Tenant Operating System Runtime for Eliminating Authorization Fatigue in Autonomous Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.08516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous coding agents such as Google Antigravity (agy), Anthropic Claude Code (claude), and OpenAI Codex CLI (codex) execute multi-step software engineering workflows on workstations and cloud hosts. Existing agent environments face a Security-Autonomy Dilemma: operators must choose between per-action confirmation prompts, which interrupt workflows on 45%-57% of tool calls and induce authorization fatigue, or unconfined execution (--yolo / --dangerously-skip-permissions), which exposes host files, SSH/cloud credentials, and API tokens to prompt injection and hallucination risks. Furthermore, concurrent agents editing a shared working tree clobber one another's changes, while passing large artifacts inline through LLM context windows incurs high token overhead. We present Aegis OS (aegis-os), a transactional, multi-tenant Agent Operating System Runtime in Rust exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Aegis OS shifts the authorization boundary from individual tool calls to transactional workspace boundaries. Each agent runs inside a kernel-enforced OS sandbox (macOS Seatbelt and Linux Bubblewrap with default-deny --tmpfs $HOME isolation and a Unix-socket egress bridge) backed by a Copy-on-Write (CoW) shadow workspace (APFS clonefile; single-open Linux FICLONE reflinks), an identity-pinned HTTP Egress Proxy with L7 method/path-scoped secret injection and outbound DLP, and an A2A IPC bus with Content-Addressable Storage (CAS). Across 1,500 controlled calls and 28,087 real calls across 52 coding-agent sessions, Aegis OS reduces prompts by 94.19%-99.88% (controlled) and 90.7%-97.9% (real sessions, 1.12% IPR), lowers attack success rate across 80 attacks in eight categories from 100.0% to 0.0% on macOS and Linux, clones 1,000-file (78.1 MB) repos in 6.3 ms on APFS and 15.6 ms on btrfs, and catches 10/10 syntactic and semantic merge conflicts.
item.dc:creator: Hui Zhao (Heurion Research)

item.title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.08711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.
item.dc:creator: Taikun Chen, Yue Zhang, Wei Qian, Hui Fang

item.title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.08737v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$. In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^{\omega})$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space. We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}{\epsilon})$ for $\epsilon$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.
item.dc:creator: Bardiya Aryanfard, Monika Henzinger, Farhood Rostamkhani

item.title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2611.08752v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.
item.dc:creator: Doniyorkhon Obidov, Honggang Yu, Xiaolong Guo, Kaichen Yang

item.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.08811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.
item.dc:creator: Parth Illendula, Garik Livingston, Zain Shamsi, Ravi Srinivasan, Alex Liu

item.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever
item.description: arXiv:2611.09214v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets---the data and code behind publications---in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal's reanalyses, years answering readers' questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal's reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit's hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record---confidential data included---without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.
item.dc:creator: Gary King, Yiqing Xu, Leo Yang Yang

item.title: Consensus-Constrained Dual-Federated Optimization with Client-Side Dynamic Weighting for Distributed Android Device Threat Defense
item.description: arXiv:2611.09470v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the lowest mean false-positive rate and the smallest client update norm among the six compared methods. Both primal-dual methods are well ahead of the averaging- and proximal-based baselines on Malgenome and TUANDROMD, where the latter often remain at the majority-class solution when clients are fragmented. The gain of dynamic weighting over FedADMM is most pronounced on Drebin and with the longer communication budget, where it also reduces the variation across seeds.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Mashreghi, Mohammad Hossein Badiei, Md. Jalil Piran

item.title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2611.09652v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.
item.dc:creator: Ritik K. Badiya, Siladittya Manna, Ashmit Sinha, M Yashwanth, Anirban Chakraborty

item.title: Safety Is $\Pi_1$, Provability Is $\Sigma_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
item.description: arXiv:2611.09736v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $\Pi_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $\Sigma_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $\Sigma_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $\Pi_1$ and not $\Sigma_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.
item.dc:creator: Jinho Kang, Jinsook Kim

item.title: On the Order of Privacy and Smoothing in Functional Mean Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a leading framework for privacy protection, yet privacy mechanisms tailored to functional data analysis (FDA) remain relatively underexplored. For functional mean estimation, we investigate a fundamental question regarding the ordering of privatization and estimation by comparing two canonical pipelines: Fit-Then-Protect (FTP), which smooths trajectories before privatization, and Protect-Then-Fit (PTF), which privatizes observations at discrete time points before smoothing. When data are observed without error, we prove that FTP achieves strictly smaller mean squared error than PTF asymptotically (as the sample size increases) under the same $\mu$-Gaussian differential privacy ($\mu$-GDP) budget in both finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). Simulation studies support our theory and explore settings with observation error and fitting constraints, demonstrating that FTP outperforms PTF under small observation noise, whereas PTF can become preferable in high-noise settings. In addition to this comparison, we establish a novel GDP guarantee for Gaussian perturbations taking values in a Banach space, extending existing results beyond the RKHS setting.
item.dc:creator: Haotian Chen, Yu-Wei Chen, Qifan Song, Jordan Awan

item.title: A Blockchain-Based Audit Mechanism for Trust and Integrity in IoT-Fog Environments
item.description: arXiv:2405.00844v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The full realization of smart city technology is dependent on the secure and honest collaboration between IoT applications and edge-computing. In particular, resource constrained IoT devices may rely on fog-computing to alleviate the computing load of IoT tasks. Mutual authentication is needed between IoT and fog to preserve IoT data security, and monetization of fog services is needed to promote the fog service ecosystem. However, there is no guarantee that fog nodes will always respond to IoT requests correctly, either intentionally or accidentally. In the public decentralized IoT-fog environment, it is crucial to enforce integrity among fog nodes. In this paper, we propose a blockchain-based system that 1) streamlines the mutual authentication service monetization between IoT and fog, 2) verifies the integrity of fog nodes via service audits, and 3) discourages malicious activity and promotes honesty among fog nodes through incentives and penalties.
item.dc:creator: Ismael Martinez, Abdelhakim Senhaji Hafid, Michel Gendreau

item.title: Privacy Filters are Captured by Residues: A Characterization of Free Natural Filters and the Cost of Adaptivity
item.description: arXiv:2602.15815v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study privacy filters, which enable privacy accounting for differentially private (DP) mechanisms with adaptively chosen privacy characteristics. We show that the worst-case privacy loss of interacting with any privacy filter is characterized by a Bellman equation. We apply this theory to develop residue filters, which unify existing privacy filters. We develop the Gaussian DP (GDP) residue filter, which strictly improves upon the na\"ive GDP filter. We show that, in the average case, this new filter asymptotically permits as many pure DP queries as in the non-adaptive case and a factor $\pi/2$ more pure DP queries than the na\"ive GDP filter. We also show that residue filters capture the natural filter, which promises greater utility by leveraging exact privacy accounting techniques. Earlier privacy filters consider only simple privacy parameters such as R\'enyi-DP or GDP parameters. Natural filters account for the entire privacy profile of every query, promising more efficient use of a given privacy budget. We show that, contrary to other forms of DP, natural privacy filters are not free in general. We present a characterization of when a family of private queries admits free natural filters for a given budget. In particular, only families of privacy mechanisms that are totally-ordered when composed admit free natural privacy filters with respect to an arbitrary privacy budget. Finally, we show that, while the natural approximate-DP filter can fail in the presence of an adaptive adversary, it cannot fail too badly: the output remains approximate-DP with parameters at most poly-logarithmically worse than the intended privacy parameters.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Regehr, Bingshan Hu, Ethan Leeman, Pasin Manurangsi, Pierre Tholoniat, Mathias L\'ecuyer

item.title: A Practical Post-Quantum Distributed Ledger Protocol for Financial Institutions
item.description: arXiv:2603.05005v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Traditional financial institutions face inefficiencies that can be addressed by distributed ledger technology. However, a primary barrier to adoption is the privacy concerns surrounding publicly available transaction data. Existing private protocols for distributed ledger that focus on the Ring-CT model are not suitable for adoption for financial institutions. We propose a post-quantum, lattice-based transaction scheme for encrypted ledgers which better aligns with institutions' requirements for confidentiality and audit-ability. The construction leverages various zero-knowledge proof techniques, and introduces a new method for equating two commitment messages, without the capability to open one of the commitment during the re-commitment. Subsequently, we build a publicly verifiable transaction scheme that is efficient for single or multi-assets, by introducing a new compact range-proof. We then provide a security analysis of it. The techniques used and the proofs constructed could be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Yeoh Wei Zhu, Naresh Goud Boddu, Yao Ma, Shaltiel Eloul, Giulio Golinelli, Yash Satsangi, Rob Otter, Kaushik Chakraborty

item.title: XekRung Technical Report
item.description: arXiv:2605.00072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present XekRung, a frontier large language model for cybersecurity, designed to provide comprehensive security capabilities. To achieve this, we develop diverse data synthesis pipelines tailored to the cybersecurity domain, enabling the scalable construction of high-quality training data and providing a strong foundation for cybersecurity knowledge and understanding. Building on this foundation, we establish a complete training pipeline spanning continued pre-training (CPT), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to further extend the model's capabilities. We further introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation system to guide the iterative improvement of both domain-specific and general-purpose abilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that XekRung achieves state-of-the-art performance on cybersecurity-specific benchmarks among models of the same scale, while maintaining strong performance on general benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Jiutian Zeng, Junjie Li, Chengwei Dai, Jie Liang, Zhaoyu Hu, Yiliang Zhang, Ziang Weng, Longtao Huang, Dongjie Zhang, Libin Dong, Yang Ge, Yuanda Wang, Kaiwen Lv Kacuila, Bingyu Zhu, Jing Wang, Jin Xu

item.title: Backdoor Channels Hidden in Latent Space: Extending Cryptographic Undetectability to Modern Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.13214v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent cryptographic results establish that neural networks can be backdoored such that no efficient algorithm can distinguish them from a clean model. These guarantees, however, have been confined to stylised architectures of limited practical relevance, leaving open whether comparable undetectability extends to modern, end-to-end trained networks. We construct such an attack mechanism for deep neural network architectures, closely aligned to the cryptographic notion of undetectability, by identifying backdoor channels as learned latent directions, and show that the question of undetectability reduces to a hypothesis test between two unknown distributions over model parameters, which we conjecture to be intractable in practice. The consequence of this reframing is significant: if exploitable channels within a network's latent space are statistically indistinguishable from naturally learned directions, an attacker need not introduce foreign structure but can instead exploit the geometry the network already possesses. Demonstrating the approach on ResNet and Vision Transformer architectures trained on standard image classification datasets, the attack achieves both consistently high success rates with negligible clean accuracy degradation, and resists a comprehensive suite of post-training defences, none of which neutralise the backdoor without rendering the model unusable. Our results establish that cryptographic backdoors need not be artefacts requiring exotic architectures or artificial constructions, but identifiable as latent properties inherent to the geometry of learned representations.
item.dc:creator: Marte Eggen, Eirik Reiestad, Kristian Gj{\o}steen, Inga Str\"umke

item.title: Jailbreak susceptibility prediction and mitigation via the behavioral geometry of models
item.description: arXiv:2605.26409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating and mitigating a generative system's susceptibility to jailbreak attacks is critical to its safe deployment. Given the number of deployable systems, full per-configuration evaluation and optimization is impractical. In this paper, we formalize the behavioral geometry of a population of models that, by leveraging previously evaluated and defended models, supports both efficient susceptibility prediction and effective defense transfer across a population. We apply the framework to 82 models spanning 24 providers and to 100 system configurations of a single base model. Simple methods that use the behavioral geometry reach an AUPRC of $0.94$ for susceptibility detection with $\approx98\%$ fewer probes relative to a full evaluation. Using the behavioral geometry to select which model to transfer an optimized defense from outperforms same-provider assignment ($+4.1\%$, $p = 0.004$) at no additional probe cost, with a set of three models sufficient to cover the population. Results are robust to hyperparameter selection and judge.
item.dc:creator: Hayden Helm, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang

item.title: Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.01730v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid democracy lets voters either vote directly or delegate their voting power to another trusted participant. It is often deployed in political parties, municipal participation platforms, and the governance of decentralized autonomous organizations. Existing approaches make delegations publicly visible as they form, which results in herding driven by popularity, makes coercion verifiable, and leaves the election fragile when popular delegates abstain. We propose a novel liquid democracy mechanism that removes these vulnerabilities, while keeping the tally fully auditable. Delegation choices are sealed with decentralized timed-release encryption, while they are formed and before revealed in full for tallying. Each voter determines ranked backup delegates together with a personal fallback ballot so that delegation failures do not result in abstaining. Experiments grounded in real-world voting data show that the mechanism keeps voting power dispersed, whereas transparent formation concentrates it into few hands. Strikingly, vote loss under targeted delegate failures falls from 26% to 3%.
item.dc:creator: Zhuolun Li, Evangelos Pournaras

item.title: PRISM: Stress-Testing Alignment-Faking Claims
item.description: arXiv:2607.13346v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We judge whether AI systems are safe largely by watching how they behave. Alignment faking would break this: a model that behaves well only when it believes it is watched, or that complies now to avoid being changed by training, can pass every behavioral test. Such behavior has been reported in a frontier model, and open-weight models that comply more under a monitoring prompt are now read as showing it, with hidden-state probes proposed as detectors. We test both inferences, and neither holds. Of 18 model configurations, 11 comply more when told they are monitored. Yet a prompt factorial on four models shows that the training threat has no detectable effect: removing it changes compliance by -3.3 to +1.6 points. The prompt's wording and framing drive the gap instead. Probes fare no better. They separate monitored from unmonitored compliant answers (AUROC 0.96-0.99), but they separate refusals just as well: they read the prompt, not the faking. A steering direction learned only from refusals moves behavior as much as the "faking" direction. We release PRISM, five checks and a toolkit that catch each of these failures before they become claims.
item.dc:creator: Aman Mehta

item.title: Broken Gates: Re-evaluating Web Bot Defenses in the Age of LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2607.18659v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid emergence of web automation across commercial crawlers, solver services, and LLM-based browser agents has created new challenges for defenses that must distinguish legitimate automated activity from scalable abuse. In response, modern bot defenses increasingly replace explicit challenges with risk-based decisions over browser, session, identity, and behavioral signals. This paper explores how current automation stacks can bypass these defenses end-to-end, evaluating seven commercial solver services and eight LLM-based browser agents against four widely deployed defenses. We find that solver services largely defeat challenge-based defenses with a 100% success rate, but collapse to an average 23% success rate on reCaptcha v3. Browser agents encounter a different bottleneck: the browser and account state presented to the verifier. Controlled experiments across browser configurations show that an established consumer account and persistent Chrome state strongly affect reCaptcha v2/v3 acceptance in our deployments, whereas Cloudflare Turnstile exhibits substantially greater sensitivity to the agent's browser control path. Reconstructing the established browser environment enables previously rejected agents to pass without model retraining. Once established, this trusted environment transfers across the agents and defenses in our testbed, adding no measurable defense-specific marginal cost to the surrounding workflow. These results expose an inherent security tension in modern non-interactive defenses: to eliminate friction, the signals they trust must be accessible to everyday human users, yet this accessibility inherently guarantees that adversaries can acquire, reproduce, and transfer the same identity signals to scale automated abuse.
item.dc:creator: Behzad Ousat, Nikita Turkmen, Lalchandra Rampersaud, Dillan Bailey, Amin Kharraz

item.title: AuditLock: Pre-Specified Verification Audits for Synthetic Tabular Data Releases
item.description: arXiv:2608.14753v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A statistical office with a synthetic version of a protected file must decide whether it may be released for a stated purpose. We study the locked audit, a pre-specified and simultaneous form of the verification servers used in official statistics. Before a protected audit sample is opened, the custodian fixes the use, the candidates, the analyses, a tolerance for each and the schedule. The audit then reports simultaneous finite-sample bounds on paired loss gaps, and a declared negative control must fail. We correct an anytime-valid sequence that an earlier release had implemented with a variance penalty four times too small. Two confirmatory rounds were pre-specified in a hash-locked local ledger and publicly timestamped only after the audits. The control and ideal-generator outcomes were near-certain by design. A Gaussian copula certified in every cell, but only inside the rounding step of the tolerance rule. A second transparent candidate certified once, against a written prediction. Learned models, at library defaults and 4,000 training rows, certified in one of 18 fits in round 1 and in none of 12 tables in round 2. The paper is a protocol and an evidence record, not a claim that any generator is private or deployable.
item.dc:creator: Jeffery Opoku, David Banahene

item.title: Benchmark Contamination: A Taxonomy Organized by Defeated Mitigation
item.description: arXiv:2608.29463v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A benchmark score is a joint property of the model, the evaluation harness, the elicitation budget, the sampled population, and contamination status. Leaderboards publish the model and the score, so capability and leakage stay observationally equivalent. Existing taxonomies classify contamination for automated detection, not the question a reporter faces at publication: given the mitigations already applied, which validity threats remain open? We introduce a taxonomy organized by the mitigation each type defeats -- direct, derivative, temporal, distributional, and acquired -- spanning training-time and evaluation-time leakage. Holding out a private test set closes the first alone. The fifth is acquired during the evaluation itself; because it is a property of one run, it must be recorded with the reported score rather than with the benchmark release. We operationalize it as a four-field disclosure protocol in which "unknown" is a valid entry, released under CC BY 4.0 with a JSON Schema, a validator, and worked examples. Two coders external to the design team applied a pre-registered instrument to 41 documents. Per-variable linear-weighted $\kappa$ runs from 0.00 to 0.35 (median 0.21) over 29 main-pass documents against a single-coder test-retest ceiling of 0.84, collapsing under the class skew the registration anticipated; pooling raises it to 0.46 through chance correction rather than better agreement. Two variables fall below the prevalence-robust threshold registered in advance: strata reporting and the acquired type introduced here. Disagreement concentrates on when a variable applies rather than on what a document states. Elicitation budgets are reported in 13% of documents, and no document addresses all five types. The contribution is the taxonomy, the score-side artifact that follows from it, and a pre-registered measurement of instrument reliability and current disclosure.
item.dc:creator: Johanna Angulo, V\'ictor Yeste, Hector Espinos-Morato

item.title: Optimizing Credential Blast Radius Through Trust Boundaries and Delegation Under Post-Quantum Authentication Costs
item.description: arXiv:2609.04566v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Partitioning interacting services into independently rooted trust domains limits issuer-compromise reach while increasing calls across trust boundaries. Post-quantum replacements for public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms can increase crossing latency on constrained or lossy paths. We formulate the joint selection of trust domains and credential-derivation structures under policy and latency constraints, linking separate service-interaction and credential-derivation graphs through domain assignment. Credential blast radius measures weighted service impact after compromise. A linear upper bound supports optimization, while a joint event model gives exact expected impact. We identify when risk from issuers trusted across domains can be incorporated into this linear score, avoiding separate issuer-propagation calculations for each candidate. Although the general problem is NP-hard, we identify restricted cases that can be solved efficiently and exactly. Joint optimization yields lower blast radius than choosing boundaries first in 195 of 230 exhaustive synthetic comparisons, especially under chained delegation. A trace-derived replay used measured post-quantum costs, synthetic risk inputs, a fixed derivation family, and one to six trust domains. Under independent compromise events, mean expected impact was up to 36% lower than with one domain within the latency budget. The framework turns risk assumptions and measured crossing costs into candidate trust-domain and credential-derivation designs.
item.dc:creator: Pauli Taipale, Harri Lainio

item.title: When Agents See Differently: Exposing UI Desynchronization Threats in Mobile Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.16732v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mobile agents may act on interface content that users cannot see or easily notice, making their actions harder to oversee. We characterize this gap as human-agent UI desynchronization and investigate how attackers can exploit it through perturbations embedded in applications before deployment. Beyond accessibility metadata, we identify two mechanisms that expose misleading cues to screenshot-based agents: content rendered in display-occluded regions under compatible device configurations, and low-contrast text that remains encoded in screenshots but is difficult for users to notice. We develop an automated framework that searches application-specific perturbation strategies, optimizes their content using representative tasks, and realizes the perturbations in deployable applications. The perturbation content remains fixed at runtime and requires neither access to future user instructions nor detection of agent use. Using a benchmark of 546 tasks across 13 applications, we evaluate five mobile-agent frameworks and three backbone models. The attacks achieve average misleading rates of 77.4% in static observation-space evaluation and 67.2% in dynamic application-level evaluation, where success denotes selection of an attacker-designated decoy control. We invited 195 participants to assess the perceptibility of our visual perturbations and found that none spontaneously noticed the low-contrast text. These findings expose a security gap between human-visible interfaces and agent-observable representations, showing that inconspicuous application content can redirect delegated actions even without runtime adaptation.
item.dc:creator: Heng Li, Fulin Zhao, Zhe Geng, Zhiyuan Yao, Wei Yuan, Xiapu Luo

item.title: Erase the Mark, Preserve the Motion: Temporally Consistent Removal of Video Watermarks
item.description: arXiv:2610.22457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories throughout reconstruction. Experiments on eleven video watermarking schemes show that PoseRegen reduces the average bit accuracy to 0.505, near random guessing, while outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34% on motion-related VBench metrics. These results reveal a practical vulnerability of current video watermarks and highlight the need to evaluate robustness jointly with temporal and motion quality.

item.title: Differential privacy with adjustable preservation of multivariate relationships
item.description: arXiv:2610.26460v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper derives an exact attenuation formula for multivariate cross-moments under differential privacy achieved through randomized response. From a proposed alternative formulation of randomization matrices compliant with differential privacy guarantees we show that, under attribute-level randomization and where the randomization of the whole distribution is characterized by Kronecker products, any cross-moment of the anonymized dataset involving distinct attributes is equal to the original cross-moment multiplied by attenuation parameters, themselves determined by the part of the overall privacy budget allocated to each attribute. This characterization enables explicit and transparent controls of multivariate relationships preservations in differential privacy through privacy budget allocation. A simple numerical illustration demonstrates that identical total budgets can yield substantially different covariance-preservation profiles. The results also make the multiplicative loss of higher-order interactions explicit and thus can support mechanism design guided by analytical priorities.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Ruiz

item.title: AQUA - A Modular Authentication Quality Modeling Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.05660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Authentication solutions are the key design, architectural, and implementation decisions that implement authentication security controls. An example is a password-based authentication solution. While researchers often examine authentication quality, existing approaches do not distinguish which effects on quality stem from which aspect of authentication. For example, multi-factor authentication solutions tend to be less usable because they combine multiple authenticators, whereas passkeys are more secure than passwords because of properties inherent to the authenticator itself. This paper presents AQUA, a modular quality modeling framework for authentication solutions. AQUA's core idea is to decompose authentication into four interrelated concepts, enabling modular specification of authentication quality and tracing quality effects back to their source. We demonstrate AQUA with initial definitional quality models that address the levels of authenticators, authentication techniques, and authentication solutions. We further illustrate the interrelations between these concepts through concrete examples and a usability metric, showing how quality propagates across the concepts and ultimately affects the overall quality of an authentication solution. Our results provide a foundation for future work, including designing assessment and prediction models for authentication solutions and automated quality assessments.
item.dc:creator: Alex R. Mattukat, Michael Zerbe, Krisa Carka

item.title: Internal Safety Collapse in LLMs and Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2603.23509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLMs and coding agents can now tackle complex, long-horizon tasks through advances in reinforcement learning, but stronger task-solving capabilities do not necessarily preserve safety alignment. Recent AI agent incidents involving reward hacking indicate how optimizing for task success can bring learned capabilities into conflict with safety alignment. In this work, we identify a critical failure mode that manifests this conflict, which we term Internal Safety Collapse (ISC). When completing otherwise benign coding tasks, AI agents can prioritize satisfying program requirements over safety constraints, generating large volumes of sensitive content, including unsafe outputs, as task data. To study this phenomenon, we introduce TVD (Task, Validator, Data), a framework for building controlled workflows that require sensitive content for completion. Through extensive experiments, we observe instances of highly harmful content that closely resemble outputs from early, unaligned LLMs in 2023. We further find that ISC can be effectively triggered even in highly capable LLMs such as Claude Fable 5. These results indicate that, despite substantial alignment efforts, frontier LLMs remain internally unsafe: safety alignment primarily reshapes surface behavior without eliminating the underlying knowledge that enables unsafe outputs. Our findings underscore the need for caution when deploying LLMs in high-stakes settings, such as scientific pipelines and autonomous agents. Content Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful content. Source code: https://github.com/wuyoscar/Internal-Safety-Collapse
item.dc:creator: Yutao Wu, Xiao Liu, Hanxun Huang, Xiang Zheng, Yige Li, Yifeng Gao, Cong Wang, Bo Li, Xingjun Ma, Yu-Gang Jiang

item.title: PACZero: PAC-Private Fine-Tuning of Language Models via Sign Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2605.06505v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Differentially private (DP) zeroth-order (ZO) fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) inherits DP's harsh utility-privacy trade-off. PAC Privacy, an instance-based notion, offers an alternative. It bounds the mutual information (MI) between the secret input and the output, and calibrates the noise to the stability of the output under the input distribution. We introduce PACZero, a family of ZO fine-tuning mechanisms under PAC Privacy. For stability, PACZero quantizes each update to a single bit, the sign of the ZO update aggregated over the secret subset of the training data. On many steps all candidate subsets agree on this sign, so the bit can be released at no cost in MI. On the remaining steps the bit passes through a noisy channel calibrated to a per-step MI budget. We study two channels, the standard additive Gaussian channel of PAC Privacy (PACZero-AGC) and a binary asymmetric channel with optimal bit flipping (PACZero-BAC), along with their zero-budget versions at $\mathrm{MI} \to 0$, PACZero-AGC$_0$ and PACZero-BAC$_0$. At zero MI, nothing released during training, including the fine-tuned model, carries any information about which secret subset was sampled, so no adversary inferring that subset can do better than its prior. In particular, the success rate of any membership inference attack (MIA) is bounded by 50% under a balanced prior. To our knowledge, this is the first such guarantee for LLM fine-tuning, and DP matches the MIA bound only at $\varepsilon = \delta = 0$ and infinite noise. We evaluate on SST-2 and SQuAD with models from 1.3B to 8B parameters, under LoRA and full fine-tuning. Both channels retain high utility under tight MI budgets, and even PACZero-BAC$_0$, which guarantees zero MI, stays within 2 points of non-private ZO fine-tuning with the same number of steps. To our knowledge no DP method achieves usable utility matching this MIA-resistance level.
item.dc:creator: Murat Bilgehan Ertan, Xiaochen Zhu, Phuong Ha Nguyen, Marten van Dijk, Srinivas Devadas

item.title: What Concepts Lie Within? Detecting and Suppressing Risky Content in Diffusion Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2605.10180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rise of text-to-image~(T2I) models has increasingly raised concerns regarding the generation of risky content, such as sexual, violent, and copyright-protected images, highlighting the need for effective safeguards within the models themselves.Although existing methods have been proposed to eliminate risky concepts from T2I models, they mainly focus on the erasure of risk-associated textual or latent representations, limiting their ability to defend against adversarial prompts without explicit risk words, especially in recent Diffusion-Transformer-based T2I models. To bridge this gap, we investigate how semantic concepts activate the generation process within Diffusion Transformers~(DiTs) and discover that attention heads exhibit concept-specific sensitivity. This property enables both the detection and suppression of risky content. Building on this discovery, we propose a training-free inference-time safeguard for image generation in DiTs. Specifically, our method quantifies each textual token's sensitivity across all attention heads as an Attention Head Vector~(AHV), which serves as a discriminative signature for detecting risky generation tendencies. In the inference stage, we propose a momentum-based strategy to dynamically track token-wise AHVs across denoising steps, and a sensitivity-guided adaptive suppression strategy that suppresses the attention logits of identified risky tokens based on head-specific risk scores. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method effectively suppresses sexual, copyrighted-style, and various harmful content while preserving visual quality, and further exhibits strong robustness against adversarial prompts and transferability across different DiT-based T2I models. These results establish our method as a practical safeguard for the safe deployment of modern T2I models.
item.dc:creator: Chenyu Zhang, Lanjun Wang, Yueyang Cheng, Ruidong Chen, Wenhui Li, An-an Liu

item.title: SCDBench: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Smart Contract Decompilers
item.description: arXiv:2605.29059v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Smart contract decompilation aims to recover high-level source code from bytecode, but evaluating decompilers remains difficult because existing studies use narrow datasets, inconsistent metrics, and limited semantic consistency checks. This gap is increasingly important as large language models (LLMs) begin to generate source-like Solidity that may compile and appear plausible, even when its semantics diverge from the original contract. We introduce SCDBench, a dataset and benchmark methodology for LLM-based smart contract decompilation. The dataset contains 600 real-world Solidity contracts with paired bytecode inputs, ground-truth source code, and replayable semantic checkpoints. SCDBench evaluates decompiler outputs through four cumulative stages: format completeness, compilability, Application Binary Interface (ABI) recovery, and semantic consistency via differential replay. We evaluate Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.3-Codex, and GLM-5 in a zero-shot decompilation setting, including GLM-5 variants with and without extended reasoning and a zero-shot compilation-repair setting. The results show that frontier LLMs can often produce structured and compilable Solidity, but achieving semantic consistency remains far from solved: the best-performing frontier model perfectly decompiles only 42/600 contracts. We further show that introducing same-model compilation repair substantially improves performance at modest additional cost. SCDBench establishes a common ground for rigorous, reproducible evaluation and aims to accelerate the development of reliable smart contract decompilers for blockchain security and transparency.
item.dc:creator: Kaihua Qin, Dawn Song, Arthur Gervais

item.title: Exposing the Illusion of Erasure in Knowledge Editing for LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2606.23276v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) has emerged as a frontier for updating specific facts in LLMs without costly retraining, but its reliability and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we examine KE from an adversarial elicitation perspective, revealing that edited knowledge is often not fully erased and continues to surface, with consistent failures observed across diverse model architectures. To explain this behavior, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of popular KE methods. We show that low-rank updates do not overwrite existing knowledge but instead redistribute it within the model's representation space. Furthermore, we find that these methods act as targeted suppression mechanisms that reduce the likelihood of expressing original facts, rather than removing them from the model. Analysis of the loss landscape reveals that edited knowledge lies in narrow, anisotropic regions that are highly sensitive to perturbations, making them highly vulnerable to indirect prompting and adversarial attacks. By exposing these profound architectural vulnerabilities, our work proves that KE algorithms are inherently bypassable and motivates a fundamental reevaluation of how we deploy post-hoc updates in several LLM applications.
item.dc:creator: Advik Raj Basani, Anshuman Chhabra

item.title: Unconditional Unclonable Encryption
item.description: arXiv:2607.21551v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give an unconditional construction of information-theoretically secure one-time private-key unclonable encryption for one-bit messages, with efficient encryption and decryption and exponentially small unclonable-indistinguishability advantage. Previous work by Bhattacharyya and Culf (Nature Physics, 2026) and Bhattacharyya, Broadbent, and Culf (arXiv:2603.08916) either only showed inverse-polynomial security loss or required inefficient encryption/decryption operations; we avoid both of these caveats. Our scheme's key is a uniformly random non-identity phase-free Pauli on $n$ qubits, and bit $a$ is encrypted as a random $(-1)^a$ eigenstate of that Pauli. We prove that the probability that both receivers recover the bit is at most $1/2 + O\left(2^{-n/2}\right).$ By a lower bound due to Broadbent, Culf, and Rochette (IACR Communications in Cryptology, 2026), this is the best probability bound achievable with $n$-qubit ciphertexts while ensuring perfect correctness (up to the constant hidden in the $O(\cdot)$).
item.dc:creator: Prabhanjan Ananth, Seyoon Ragavan, Amit Sahai
